newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ sees resolution of Iran diplomatic row soon.
newsitem.headline: NZ sees resolution of Iran diplomatic row soon.

text.p: New Zealand's foreign minister Don McKinnon said on Tuesday he expected confusion over a reported trade ban imposed by Iran to be resolved in days.
"I think by the end of the week it'll be resolved. So far, as I understand it it's not affecting any New Zealand exports", McKinnon told Radio New Zealand.
The reported boycott was sparked by New Zealand recalling its ambassador to Tehran after a German court ruling linking Iran to the 1992 murders of four Kurdish terrorists in Berlin.
McKinnon, who met Iran's ambassador Mohammad Sazegara for talks late on Monday, said the envoy told him he had not received any formal advice from Iran of a trade ban.
Earlier on Monday, the Iranian embassy appeared to confirm that the trade ban, first reported by the official news agency IRNA on Saturday, was already in place.
Sazegara left Wellington for Tehran on Tuesday, an embassy spokesman told Reuters.
McKinnon said the New Zealand ambassador to Tehran, Daniel Richards, would be back in Iran by the end of the week and talks would go on.
Wellington's morning mewspaper on Tuesday asked whether Iran had picked on New Zealand because it was a softer target than Germany.

"The suspicion must be that New Zealand, with exports of NZ$170 million to Iran last year and few imports, is an easier target for economic punishment than Germany," an editorial in The Dominion daily newspaper said.
It said it would be ironic for New Zealand to be singled out because it had resisted pressure to join boycotts against Iran in the past.
The paper said New Zealand separated economic from political issues and only imposed trade sanctions when they had been adopted by the United Nations or the Commonwealth.

New Zealand's top-selling daily, The New Zealand Herald, took a more philosophical approach, saying if Tehran over-reacted to a relatively low-level sign of diplomatic displeasure there was little that could be done about it.
Both papers alluded to the French sinking of the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour in 1985, to underline New Zealand's stance on state-sponsored violence.
The Iranian embassy said Sazegara would seek to meet up with Richards in Tehran in a few days' time "with a view to normalising the relations between both countries on the basis of mutual respect".
Since the row broke out at the weekend, some of New Zealand's primary exporters have expressed concern about the effects of a full-scale ban on their agricultural produce trade.

The trade, mainly selling lamb, dairy produce and wool to Iran, is not large in overall terms, totalling an estimated NZ$170 million ($119 million) last year. But if suspended it could cause short-term problems, producers said.
